justification_text:
The point estimates in the forecast reflect our best guess of the central value—449.53—in the context of the data and trends available at the time of forecasting. These estimates assume no significant surprises or deviations from the underlying trends driving the variable in question. Importantly, we kept the point estimate constant across all time horizons because there was no compelling evidence to suggest a directional bias over time. Essentially, the baseline logic assumes that, on average, the variable will revert to this central value, all else being equal. Longer horizons, however, introduce the potential for wider deviations, which brings us to the confidence intervals.

The widths of the confidence intervals are a direct reflection of increasing uncertainty over time. In the very short term, such as the 1-day horizon, variability is relatively limited since fewer outside factors have time to play a role. Thus, the 90% confidence interval of 443.79 to 455.27 is reasonably narrow. However, as the time horizon extends to one week or one month, more sources of randomness and variability come into play. These could include market dynamics, economic shifts, individual behavioral changes, or even unforeseen news or events. The further out we forecast, the harder it is to predict with certainty, leading to wider intervals (e.g., 419.05 to 480.01 for the 1-month horizon). 

Beyond the modeled uncertainty, there are always external risks or events that could cause outcomes to fall outside the stated intervals. These might include rare but impactful shocks such as geopolitical crises, unexpected regulatory changes, natural disasters, or even technological breakthroughs, depending on the context of what this variable represents. Events like these are difficult to quantify in advance and may create outcomes that deviate significantly from historical trends. Thus, while the forecast incorporates a wide range of normal variability, highly unusual or extreme events remain a possibility that lies outside the modeled confidence bands.
